foodDescription: Bacon, sausage, egg and black pudding, but what makes it Ulster is the bread: a soda farl and a slice of potato bread, both fried in the pan fat until golden. Beans are a point of dispute. Eaten late morning, followed by nothing until dinner.

Soda bread dough patted into a round, cut in four and cooked on a dry griddle rather than baked, so it comes out flat, floury and soft inside. Farl is from an old word for a quarter. Split it, fry it, and fill it with bacon or an egg.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin and cut into triangles, then browned on a griddle. Also called fadge or tattie bread. Unlike boxty it uses cooked potato only. Fried in butter it goes crisp and chewy at the same time.

Mashed potato beaten with hot milk and chopped scallions, piled up with a well of butter melting in the middle. Not colcannon, which has cabbage or kale; Ulster cooks will explain the difference unasked. Served beside sausages or boiled ham.

A big, round, soft white roll dusted in flour, with a dark crust on top that looks close to burnt. Bakeries pile them in the window. Split one for a bacon or sausage bap, or for a pastie bap, which is exactly what it sounds like.

A pastie here is no Cornish pasty: it is a round patty of minced pork, onion and potato, battered and deep-fried. Supper means it comes with chips. A Belfast chip shop order that needs salt, vinegar and nothing more complicated.

A ring doughnut, fried and rolled in sugar, under the name every Northern Irish bakery uses. Plain dough, no filling, no icing. Best still warm from the fryer, with a cup of tea, and a napkin for the sugar that will end up down your front.

A no-bake traybake of fifteen crushed digestive biscuits, fifteen marshmallows and fifteen glacé cherries, bound with condensed milk and rolled in coconut. Chilled and sliced. Sold in every café cabinet and nobody has ever needed a recipe card for it.

A domed bun between bread and sponge cake, with a crackled sugar top and sometimes a cherry or a few currants. Despite the name it has nothing to do with France. A Belfast bakery staple, cut in half and buttered by those who think it needs it.

Hard, golden honeycomb toffee made with golden syrup and baking soda, broken off the block with a hammer. Sold most famously at the Ould Lammas Fair in Ballycastle each August. Gets into your teeth and stays there; that is part of the deal.

Red seaweed gathered off the north Antrim coast and dried until leathery, then eaten straight from the bag as a salty snack. Traditionally paired with yellowman at the Lammas Fair. Look for it at St George’s Market. The taste is the sea, concentrated.

The first new potatoes of the year, grown in the light soil around Comber in County Down and with protected-name status since 2012. Thin-skinned and waxy, in shops from early summer. Boil them, add butter and salt, and that is the whole recipe.

Irish whiskey from the Old Bushmills Distillery on the north Antrim coast, which points to a 1608 royal licence to distil in the area. Triple-distilled and smooth. Ask for it neat or with a drop of water; Belfast bars stock several ages of it.

Northern Ireland’s own Tayto, made since 1956 at Tandragee Castle in County Armagh and unrelated to the Tayto brand in the Republic. Cheese and onion is the flagship flavour. A crisp sandwich in buttered white bread is a respected local lunch.

A dark, sticky malted loaf that has almost disappeared everywhere except Northern Ireland. Sold sliced in supermarkets, it is eaten toasted with plenty of butter and often a slice of cheese. Slightly sweet, slightly bitter, and best toasted.
